name: Gilgamesh: A New Translation of the Ancient Epic, with Essays on the Poem, Its Past, and Its Passion (Yale University Press, trans. Sophus Helle)
date: 2021 (Yale University Press hardcover, ISBN 9780300251180, xxx + 286 pp.); paperback ISBN 9780300268096 [uncertain: paperback year, probably 2022]. Preceded by the Danish verse translation Gilgamesh (Gyldendal, April 2019) made with his father, the poet Morten Søndergaard
creator: Sophus Helle, Danish Assyriologist and literary scholar (PhD Aarhus University; later postdoctoral work at Freie Universität Berlin) [uncertain: affiliation at time of publication]. Book design and the raised-dot convention for gaps developed with the design firm Wrong Studio
form: Verse translation of the Standard Babylonian epic in twelve tablets, each tablet titled by its opening words (Tablet I 'He who saw the deep', Tablet XII 'Had I only left'), with an introduction, a note on the translation, five interpretive essays ('A Poem for the Ages', 'Study the Brickwork', 'The Storm of His Heart', 'Dying to Be Read', 'Kings, Women, Monsters'), notes and bibliography
translator_access: Direct. Helle reads Akkadian and translates straight from it, without a crib. The English grew out of the earlier Danish version made with Morten Søndergaard, and Helle describes the two as shaping each other through 'inter-translational dialogue' (Full Stop interview, 2022). His base text follows Andrew George's 2003 critical edition plus fragments published since [uncertain: exact list of post-2003 sources used]
scholarly_adviser: N/A: Helle is himself the Assyriologist. The poet in the partnership is Morten Søndergaard, co-translator of the 2019 Danish version, not the English one
versions_used: Standard Babylonian as the spine, including Tablet XII. Where the Standard text is lost, scenes are filled from older versions: the Old Babylonian version and the Ugaritic version are named in margin notes (Macfarlane, NYRB 2022). Tamara Agha-Jaffar's review notes he identifies Old Babylonian passages 'when the versions differ'. The Sulaymaniyah Tablet V fragment (Al-Rawi and George 2014) appears to be incorporated in the Cedar Forest episode: Macfarlane quotes the trees 'webbed with creepers' and resin that 'fell like raindrops', details known only from that tablet [uncertain: whether all newly identified eBL fragments are used]. The Sumerian Bilgames poems are discussed in the essays, not translated as separate texts
non_standard_material: Merged into the running text but flagged. Passages inserted from older versions carry small-capital margin notes such as 'old babylonian version' or 'ugaritic version' (Macfarlane, NYRB, 20 October 2022), so the reader can see the switch without the story stopping. This is the same approach Andrew George takes, but with lighter typography
gap_policy: Bridged where scholars can reasonably reconstruct, shown where they cannot. Helle's note: 'Words that are ambiguous, implicit, emended, or reconstructed appear in regular typeface, giving my best guess at what the text once said.' So reconstructions are not distinguished from surviving text, unlike George or Foster. Genuinely lost text is still marked, and when the number of lost lines is known, that many lines are left blank. Helle has said he values some gaps as meaning in themselves: 'The absence of text as Enkidu dies is very powerful to me' (Full Stop, 2022)
typography_of_absence: No square brackets and no italics. A raised dot (like a hovering full stop) marks the start and end of a broken passage, and whole blank lines stand in for lines whose count is known. The convention came out of sessions with Wrong Studio designers and Helle's students, who tested alternatives including redaction-style black bars. Macfarlane says it gives 'a relatively smooth linear journey through the poem, without ignoring the existence of the voids'. In the Danish audiobook Søndergaard knocked with a finger to voice the gaps (Thin End of the Wedge podcast, episode 28)
tablet_xii: Included and translated as the twelfth tablet ('Had I only left'), Enkidu's descent to and report from the underworld. Helle treats it as an appendix narratively disjunct from Tablets I to XI, a partial Akkadian rendering of the Sumerian 'Bilgames and the Netherworld' [uncertain: exact wording of his framing]. The effect is that the book keeps two endings. His essays argue the true close is the walls of Uruk in Tablet XI, which loops back to the prologue, with Tablet XII as a coda on death
turning_point: Enkidu's death is the emotional hinge. Helle singles out the break in the tablet as Enkidu dies as one of the most powerful moments, precisely because text is missing. But his structural reading places the real turn at the end: Gilgamesh's return to Uruk and his command to Ur-shanabi to study the brickwork, which sends the reader back to the prologue. The essay 'Study the Brickwork' treats the wall as the poem's key image, and 'Dying to Be Read' ties the failed quest for eternal life to the survival of the written story. So the snake and Uta-napishti's sleep test close off the physical quest, while the walls of Uruk convert failure into something that lasts
arc_interpretation: A loop rather than a straight line, from grief to a kind of mortal wisdom expressed through writing and building. Evidence: (1) Helle argues the wording at the end 'far from being abrupt, is designed to lead us back to its beginning', like 'a snake biting its tail' (Agha-Jaffar review, 2022); (2) he reads the prologue as revealing Gilgamesh as the narrator who set the story down on a tablet, so the king who could not live forever lives on as a text ('Dying to Be Read'); (3) 'The Storm of His Heart' reads the poem through violent, obscure emotions, with Gilgamesh's restlessness and grief as the engine; (4) 'Kings, Women, Monsters' ties the story to kingship and power, including the tyranny the poem opens with. Helle also stresses that Gilgamesh and Enkidu 'do not explicate the nature of their feelings for one another', leaving the bond undefined rather than labelling it
key_passages: Enkidu's creation: 'a man all muscle, the mightiest in the land, / as mighty as a meteorite fallen from the sky' (quoted in Macfarlane, NYRB 2022). Shamhat and Enkidu: rendered frankly; the seven days and nights of coupling are kept [uncertain: exact wording]. Siduri: her carpe diem advice comes from the Old Babylonian Sippar tablet and is flagged with an 'old babylonian version' margin note [uncertain: exact wording and placement]. Death in the bedchamber (Tablet XI): 'The Thief of Life has a hold on my heart. / Death is sitting in my bedroom' (quoted in Macfarlane, NYRB 2022). Walls of Uruk (Tablet XI): Gilgamesh tells Ur-shanabi to climb the wall and study the brickwork; the passage echoes the prologue word for word and gives the essay 'Study the Brickwork' its title [uncertain: exact wording]. Cedar Forest (Tablet V): 'Then the cedar cast its shadow and terror fell on Gilgamesh' (read by Helle, Thin End of the Wedge ep. 28)
diction_and_metre: Free verse in modern, plain English, roughly one English line per Akkadian line, keeping the couplet parallelism and repetitions. No rhyme, no archaism. Helle aims at 'aural patterning' in place of the original's alliteration and assonance, e.g. 'work his words' for a common Akkadian phrase, to recreate 'the sinuous and sonorous pleasure of the poem' (NYRB). Macfarlane calls it 'lively, earthy' and occasionally finds the 'folksy plain speaking' in the essays too much
sample_line: "The Thief of Life has a hold on my heart. / Death is sitting in my bedroom." (Tablet XI, Helle 2021, quoted in Robert Macfarlane, 'A Fireball from the Sands', NYRB, 20 October 2022)
critical_response: Strongly positive. Robert Macfarlane (NYRB, 20 October 2022, 'A Fireball from the Sands'): 'lively, earthy, and scrupulous in its scholarship', placing it between George's philological version and the many 'translations of translations'. Tamara Agha-Jaffar (2022): 'brilliant, exciting translation and commentary', recommended for first-time and repeat readers. Cheryl Morgan (Salon Futura, 2023) found the introduction and essays the most interesting part and preferred it to literary versions by non-specialists. Blurbs from Alexander Beecroft ('fresh and vital translation, alive to the music') and Marshall Brown. Academic reviews in Zeitschrift für Assyriologie 114 (2024) 105-106 and elsewhere recommend it to a broad audience while discussing specific difficult passages [uncertain: ZA reviewer name and detailed criticisms]. The Danish version was praised in Politiken and Information
controversies: Mild. The main scholarly objection is methodological: printing reconstructions and emendations in regular type means readers cannot tell surviving text from Helle's guesses, a departure from the bracket conventions of George and Foster (discussed in the eharding Substack review). Some reviewers query individual readings of damaged passages [uncertain: specific disputed lines]. No accuracy or authorship disputes
regional_reception: Came first in Danish (2019, with Søndergaard), where reviewers called it set to become a classic. Helle has worked with Zainab Bahrani on Gilgamesh in Iraqi modernist art, but says he does not yet read Arabic; no Arabic or Kurdish edition of his translation is known [uncertain]
ai_craft_tension: Helle's version shows where the judgement sits once the tablets are read. A model can propose likely restorations, but Helle chose to print his best guesses in plain type and keep a visible dot for what is truly gone, a design decision made with graphic designers and students, not a philological one. He also argues some gaps should stay: he would find it strange if a new manuscript filled the blank where Enkidu dies, because the silence does work in the poem. That is a reader's call about meaning. His text also depends on new finds (the Sulaymaniyah resin 'like raindrops'), and fragment-matching tools will keep supplying them, but deciding whether a recovered line enters the poem, and how it should sound, still needs a translator with an ear
essay_hooks: (1) A raised dot, 'like a hovering full stop', replaces square brackets: typography designed with Wrong Studio and tested on students (Macfarlane, NYRB 2022; Thin End of the Wedge ep. 28). (2) 'Words that are ambiguous, implicit, emended, or reconstructed appear in regular typeface, giving my best guess at what the text once said': a translator openly choosing fluency over flagging. (3) Helle on the gap as Enkidu dies: 'it would be weird to me if and when... a manuscript is found that fills out this blank space' (Full Stop, 2022). (4) His father voiced the gaps in the Danish audiobook by knocking a finger. (5) 'The Thief of Life has a hold on my heart. / Death is sitting in my bedroom.' (6) A new fragment arrived mid-translation and forced a rework of Tablet II in the Danish version. (7) The ending as 'a snake biting its tail': the walls of Uruk send you back to the first page
